a: Paul
t: Did Paul write Ephesians?
p: The letter names Paul. Many scholars doubt he wrote it; many others are sure he did.
b: The letter says it is Paul's (1:1; 3:1). The church fathers, the Muratorian list and Marcion's collection all took it as his. Since the 1800s many critics have doubted it, for five reasons: very long sentences (1:3-14 is one Greek sentence of 202 words), many words found nowhere else in Paul, a close dependence on Colossians, a view of the church and of "apostles and prophets" as a past foundation (2:20; 3:5), and a calm, general tone with no personal greetings. Lincoln, Best and Schnackenburg hold it was written by a follower after Paul's death. Barth, Hoehner, Arnold and Thielman defend Paul, often through a secretary or co-worker. This Plain English Translation follows the text and calls it Paul's letter, as the text does. The book page sets out the arguments.

a: apostle
t: Apostle: a person sent
p: Paul opens with his office: one sent out with the sender's authority.
b: The Greek apostolos means someone sent, an envoy who speaks for the one who sent him. Paul claims the title "by the will of God" and not by a human appointment (compare Galatians 1:1). The word comes back in 2:20, 3:5 and 4:11, where "apostles" are the foundation of the church and one of Christ's gifts to it. See the note at 2:20 on the question whether the office was meant to continue.

a: saints
t: The saints: God's holy people
p: Not special heroes: every member of the community, set apart for God.
b: The Greek hagioi means "holy ones", people set apart for God, and Paul uses it for every believer (1 Corinthians 1:2; Romans 1:7). It does not mean those who have been declared saints by a later church. The word builds on Israel's calling as "a people holy to the LORD" (Deuteronomy 7:6), now stretched to Gentiles. In Ephesians the saints are the whole people of God (1:15, 18; 2:19; 3:8, 18). Catholic and Orthodox teaching also honors saints in heaven; that is a later and different use of the word.

a: Ephesus
t: Ephesus: Artemis and the capital of Asia
p: The leading city of the province of Asia, with one of the Seven Wonders.
b: Ephesus was a seaport and the Roman capital of the province of Asia, and a large city; estimates of its population in Roman times run from about 33,600 to about 71,600, and an older figure of up to 225,000 is now thought unrealistic. Its great temple of Artemis, first built in the later 700s BC, rebuilt on a grander scale from about 550 BC, burned in 356 BC and rebuilt from 323 BC, and counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, drew pilgrims and made the city's wealth. Artemis was worshiped there as a mother and protector, and the city was also a center of magic, as the burning of the magic books shows (Acts 19:19). Paul worked here for about three years (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31). Later the church of Ephesus was addressed in Revelation 2:1-7 and by Ignatius. See the variant at this verse on whether the letter was written to Ephesus at all.

a: Grace to you and peace
t: Grace and peace: Greek and Hebrew together
p: Paul's usual greeting joins a Greek greeting with a Hebrew one.
b: An ordinary Greek letter began chairein, "greetings." Paul changes it to charis, "grace", and adds the Hebrew shalom, "peace", meaning well-being and a right relation to God and others. He is also echoing the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:25-26). In Ephesians grace and peace are the two ideas the letter turns on: grace in 2:5-8, peace in 2:14-17. The same formula, with "God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ", opens Romans 1:7 and most of his letters.
orig: χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη (charis hymin kai eirene)

a: Blessed be God
t: A Jewish blessing prayer
p: The letter opens with the form of a Jewish berakah, 'Blessed be God...'
b: Jewish prayer often began "Blessed be the LORD" and then told what God had done (1 Kings 8:15; Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18). Paul uses the form to open this letter, as he does in 2 Corinthians 1:3, and as 1 Peter 1:3 and Luke 1:68 do. Here the thanks-giving swells into one sentence of 202 Greek words (1:3-14), with the refrain "to the praise of his glory" at 1:6, 12 and 14. Some scholars think the passage was shaped as a hymn or liturgy; others think it is Paul's own flowing prose in the style of a prayer. The Plain English Translation cuts it into sentences but keeps its order.
r: 1 Kings 8:15; Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18; Luke 1:68; 2 Corinthians 1:3; 1 Peter 1:3

a: in the heavenly world
t: The heavenly world: a place only Ephesians names
p: Five times the letter speaks of 'the heavenly places': where Christ sits and the powers live.
b: The Greek epouranios is used of the heavenly realm, and the phrase "in the heavenlies" appears five times in Ephesians and nowhere else in Paul in this form (1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12). It is where believers are already blessed and seated with Christ (1:3; 2:6), where Christ sits above all powers (1:20), and also where the powers still act (3:10; 6:12). It is a realm of spiritual reality alongside the earth, not a future place. The Plain English Translation says "world" to keep it from sounding like a sky or a heaven only to be entered after death.

a: chose us in Christ
t: Chosen in Christ: individuals or the people?
p: Churches read 'chose us in him' very differently.
b: The verb eklegomai, "to choose for oneself", recalls Israel as God's chosen people (Deuteronomy 7:6-7; 10:15). Paul says the choice was "in Christ" and "before the foundation of the world". Does this mean God picked named individuals for salvation (Augustine, Calvin, the Reformed), or that he chose Christ as the chosen one and the people in him, so that anyone who is in Christ is chosen (Barth, many Arminians and Wesleyans), or that he chose a people for a purpose, to be holy (a common reading among scholars)? Notice that the stated aim is "to be holy and without blame", not simply to be saved. The card below sets the churches' answers side by side.
r: Deuteronomy 7:6-7; Deuteronomy 10:15; Romans 8:28-30; Romans 9:11; John 15:16; 2 Thessalonians 2:13

a: before the world was founded
t: Chosen before the world: a Jewish idea
p: Jewish writers also spoke of things planned before creation.
b: Other New Testament writers say the same of Christ and his people: the Lamb was known "in advance, before the world was founded" (1 Peter 1:20), and Jesus speaks of the Father's love for him before the world's foundation (John 17:24). Jewish thought also named things that came first in God's mind. A saying in the Talmud lists seven things created before the world: the Torah, repentance, the garden of Eden, Gehenna, the throne of glory, the temple and the name of the Messiah (Pesahim 54a). Paul's point is that the choice came before any human act, and so cannot rest on a person's record.

a: before him in love
t: 'In love': with 1:4 or with 1:5?
p: The Greek 'in love' can end verse 4 or begin verse 5; the Plain English Translation puts it with verse 4.
b: Greek had no punctuation, and "in love" can be read with what comes before (holy and without blame before him, in love) or with what comes after (in love he decided beforehand to adopt us). Some English Bibles end verse 4 with it and others begin verse 5 with it. The Plain English Translation keeps it where the Greek order puts it, at the end of verse 4. The meaning of the love also divides: our love for God and others (Eph 4:2, 15-16; 5:2) or God's love for us (2:4; Romans 5:8). Both fit the letter.

a: decided beforehand
t: 'Decided beforehand': predestination
p: The Greek proorizo is the root of the English 'predestine'.
b: The verb proorizo is built from horizo, "to mark a boundary", and the prefix "before". It means to determine in advance. It occurs in Romans 8:29-30 and 1 Corinthians 2:7 and here and in 1:11. Paul does not discuss at length whom God marks out; he says what God marked out: adoption as children, and an inheritance, through Christ. Reformed teachers read it as God's fixed decree about persons; Wesleyan teachers read it as God's choice of those he foreknew would believe, within a plan that is for all. See the card on 1:4.

a: adopted as his children
t: Adoption: a Roman legal picture
p: Paul takes a Roman law word and makes a slave or outsider into an heir.
b: The Greek huiothesia, "adoption as a child" (literally "placing as a son"), is a Greek and Roman legal term for taking someone into a family with the full rights of an heir, and Paul uses it only in Romans 8:15, 23; 9:4; Galatians 4:5 and here. In a Roman family an adoption could lift a stranger or a freed slave to a great inheritance. The Plain English Translation says "children" and not "sons" because the point is the standing, open to women and men; Paul uses "sons" because an adopted son held the heir's rights. See also 1:14.

a: the Beloved
t: The Beloved: a title for the Son
p: The Greek word is the one from Jesus' baptism: 'my beloved Son'.
b: "The Beloved" is a title found only here in Paul. It echoes the voice at Jesus' baptism, "You are my beloved Son" (Mark 1:11; compare Colossians 1:13, "the Son of his love"), and, behind that, Isaiah 42:1 and Psalm 2:7. The verb "freely gave" (echaritosen) is built on charis, "grace"; it is the same verb used of Mary in Luke 1:28. God's favor reaches us because we are in the one he loves, as a family's honor spreads to the adopted child.

a: redemption
t: Redemption: set free by a price
p: Paul's word for the Exodus-style rescue, now through Christ's blood.
b: The Greek apolytrosis belongs to the language of buying back a slave or prisoner. The Greek Old Testament uses the same family of words for the Lord's rescue of Israel from Egypt (Exodus 6:6; Deuteronomy 7:8). In Paul it is the freedom Christ's death has bought (Romans 3:24; 8:23; Colossians 1:14). In 1:14 it returns as a future event, and in 4:30 as "the day of redemption". Churches differ on who was owed the "price": the early view of a ransom paid to the devil, Anselm's satisfaction of God's honor, and the substitution view. The topic page on the atonement sets them out.

a: the mystery of his will
t: Mystery: a secret now made known
p: Paul's 'mystery' is a hidden plan that has been revealed, not a puzzle.
b: The Greek mysterion is, in the Bible, a secret of God that human beings could not find out and that he has now told. In the Greek of Daniel 2 the same word stands for the "secret" that God alone could uncover (Daniel 2:18-19, 47). Here the mystery is God's will to gather everything in Christ (1:10); in 3:3-6 it is that Gentiles are fellow heirs; in 5:32 it is the great meaning of marriage in Genesis 2:24 seen in Christ and the church. The Latin Bible translated the word sacramentum. The topic page on mystery follows the word across the Bible.

a: a plan for when the times are full
t: The plan: oikonomia
p: The Greek is a household-manager's word: the way God runs his own house.
b: The Greek oikonomia comes from oikos ("house") and nomos ("rule"): the management of a household. The English word "economy" comes from it. In this letter it appears three times, with three slightly different senses: God's plan (here), Paul's assignment to carry out that plan for the Gentiles (3:2), and the plan itself again (3:9). The "fullness of the times" (compare Galatians 4:4) is a moment God himself has set. The Plain English Translation uses "plan" here and in 3:9, and "the task of managing" at 3:2, so the reader can see the three uses.

a: to bring all things together in Christ
t: Summing up all things in Christ
p: A rare verb: to sum up, gather under one head, or renew.
b: The Greek anakephalaiosasthai is found in Paul only here and in Romans 13:9, where love "sums up" the commandments. It comes from kephalaion ("main point", "sum"), and the ear also hears kephale, "head". Readings: to sum up the whole of creation in one total; to bring everything under Christ as head (compare 1:22); to renew or restore it (so Irenaeus). Irenaeus of Lyon built a teaching on it, "recapitulation": Christ goes through Adam's story again and sets it right. The Plain English Translation's "bring together" keeps the sense of gathering and leaves the three readings open.

a: given an inheritance
t: 'We were given an inheritance' or 'we were made his inheritance'?
p: The Greek verb can mean: we received a share, or we became God's share.
b: The verb eklerothemen comes from kleros, a lot or portion. It can mean we were given a share (the Plain English Translation's choice, as in the nearby 1:14, 18 where the inheritance belongs to believers), or that we were made God's own portion, as Israel was (Deuteronomy 32:9; Deuteronomy 4:20). The Plain English Translation follows the first; commentators divide between them.

a: the first to put our hope in Christ
t: Who are 'we' and who are 'you'?
p: The 'we' of 1:3-12 and the 'you' of 1:13 may be Jewish and Gentile believers.
b: The Greek proelpizo means to hope beforehand or to be first to hope. Verse 12 says "we", and verse 13 turns to "you also". Many commentators read this as Jewish believers (we, who hoped in the Messiah first) and Gentile believers (you, who heard later). That fits Acts, where the news came to the Jews first, and 2:11-22, where "you" are Gentiles. Others read "we" as Paul and his fellow workers, or as all Christians in the letter's own voice, and "you" as the readers. The question is not decided; the letter's main point is that both are included.

a: sealed with the Holy Spirit
t: The seal: ownership and safekeeping
p: A seal showed who owned a thing and guarded it.
b: A seal, pressed into clay or wax, marked a document or property as belonging to its owner and guarded it. Here the Holy Spirit is God's seal on believers. The same image appears in 2 Corinthians 1:22 and Ephesians 4:30 (where Paul warns against making the Holy Spirit sad, the Spirit who sealed them for the day of redemption). When does the sealing happen? Paul's order here is hearing, believing, then being sealed. Churches differ: in the sacraments of initiation (baptism and confirmation for Catholics; chrismation, which follows baptism at once, for the Orthodox; the word and baptism for Lutherans), at the moment of believing (Reformed, Baptist, many evangelicals), or in a later experience of the Spirit (many Pentecostals). The card below sets the views side by side.

a: down payment
t: The Spirit as a down payment
p: The word comes from the business world: a first payment that guarantees the rest.
b: The Greek arrabon is a Semitic loanword for a first installment, a deposit that pledges the full payment and is a part of it. The Hebrew form is the pledge Judah left with Tamar (Genesis 38:17-18, where the Greek Old Testament uses the same word). In modern Greek it still means an engagement. Paul uses it for the Spirit in 2 Corinthians 1:22 and 5:5. The Spirit given now is already the first part of the coming inheritance, and a promise that the rest will follow.

a: the people God has made his own
t: God's own possession
p: A phrase drawn from Israel's calling as God's treasured people.
b: The Greek peripoiesis means something acquired for oneself. It is the word of Malachi 3:17 in the Greek Old Testament, where the people are the Lord's "possession" (Hebrew segullah). Exodus 19:5 has the same Hebrew word, which the Greek renders with the related laos periousios, and 1 Peter 2:9 has "a people God has made his own". Paul takes the vocabulary of Israel's election and applies it to the church of Jews and Gentiles. The "redemption" of this people is still ahead, at the resurrection (compare Romans 8:23), as 4:30 also says.

a: since I heard about the faith among you
t: 'I heard of your faith': did Paul know these readers?
p: Paul writes as if he knows them only by report; the letter was perhaps not for Ephesus alone.
b: Paul lived in Ephesus about three years and told the elders that for those years he warned them night and day (Acts 20:31). Yet in 1:15 he has only "heard" of their faith, and in 3:2 and 4:21 he says "if you have heard" about his task and "if you have heard about him". There are no personal greetings and no names except Tychicus (6:21). Colossians 1:4 uses almost the same phrase about a church Paul had not seen. Explanations: a letter circulated among the churches of Asia, "in Ephesus" being the copy sent to the capital (the circular-letter view, held by many); a letter by a later writer to readers he pictured in general; a letter written some years after Paul left, when most of the believers were new.

a: a spirit of wisdom and revelation
t: A spirit of wisdom: the Holy Spirit or a gift?
p: The Greek is 'a spirit', and it is unclear whether Paul means the Holy Spirit or a human attitude.
b: The Greek has no capital letters, so "a spirit of wisdom and revelation" can be read as the Holy Spirit giving wisdom (compare Isaiah 11:2, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding), or as a disposition or inner gift that the Spirit works in the reader. Some English Bibles print a capital S and some a small one; the Plain English Translation says "a spirit" because the Greek has no article and no capital. Commentators divide, and some hold that both are meant. The aim is stated: "as you come to know him". Paul asks for knowledge of God, not extra facts.

a: the eyes of your heart
t: Heart: the mind and will, not only feeling
p: In Hebrew thought the heart is where one thinks and decides.
b: The Hebrew lev and the Greek kardia, "heart", name the center of the person, where one thinks, wills and plans, and not only where one feels (Proverbs 4:23; Jeremiah 17:9). "The eyes of your heart" is a figure for inner sight. The verb "lit up" (a perfect passive participle) says that this has already been done to them. Light and darkness, sight and blindness return in 4:18 and 5:8-14. The KJV has "understanding" here.

a: his inheritance among the saints
t: Whose inheritance? God's, or ours?
p: 'The wealth of the glory of his inheritance' can mean what God gets or what we get.
b: Two readings. One: the inheritance is God's own, his people among whom he has a rich glory (Deuteronomy 32:9: "the LORD's own share is his people"), as in 1:14. Two: it is what believers will inherit from God, as at 1:11 and 5:5. The Greek "in the saints" can mean "among" or "in", which fits either. Commentators divide, and some hold the letter means both. Paul wants his readers to see how rich the whole matter is: a God who treasures his people, and a people who will share his world.

a: the work of the might of his strength
t: Four words for power
p: Paul piles up synonyms to show how much power God uses.
b: Verses 19-20 pile up four Greek words for power: dynamis (ability), energeia (active working; our word "energy"), kratos (might, strength in action) and ischys (strength). English cannot give each its own word, and Paul may simply be heaping them up, as he heaps "ruler, authority, power and lordship" in 1:21. The point is not a theory of power but its size: the same strength that raised Jesus is at work "for us who believe". The word "energy" in 3:7 and 3:20 ("working") is the same one as here.
orig: ἐνέργεια τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος (energeia tou kratous tes ischyos)

a: seated him at his right hand
t: Psalm 110:1: the king at God's right hand
p: The picture is from Psalm 110:1, the most-quoted psalm in the New Testament.
b: In Psalm 110:1 the LORD invites the king, "my lord", to sit at his right hand until his enemies are made a footstool. The New Testament uses it of the risen Jesus again and again (Acts 2:34-35; 1 Corinthians 15:25; Colossians 3:1; Hebrews 1:13). The picture is of a king given a seat next to the throne with all authority. In Ephesians, Christ's exaltation (1:20-22) is the pattern for what is said of believers in 2:6, that they are seated "with him". Psalm 8:6 is added in 1:22.

a: ruler, authority, power and lordship
t: Rulers and authorities: the powers above the world
p: Four titles of heavenly or earthly powers, all placed below Christ.
b: Paul lists arche (ruler, beginning), exousia (authority), dynamis (power) and kyriotes (lordship). Lists like this appear in Romans 8:38, 1 Corinthians 15:24, Colossians 1:16 and 2:15, and in Jewish writings about angelic orders. Most readers take them as angelic and demonic powers; some modern writers also see them in human structures such as law, money and empire. Whatever they are, Christ is far above them, "not only in this age but also in the age that is coming". The topic page on the powers sets out the views; see also 3:10 and 6:12.

a: not only in this age but also in the age that is coming
t: Two ages: a Jewish way of dividing time
p: 'This age' and 'the age to come' come from Jewish thought.
b: Jewish teachers divided time into "this age" (Hebrew olam hazeh) of sin and death, and "the age to come" (olam haba) of God's rule. Paul uses the scheme (Romans 12:2; 1 Corinthians 2:6-8; Galatians 1:4), and 4 Ezra 7:50 and 2 Baruch 44:8-15 use it too. Ephesians has a particular twist: believers are already raised and seated in the heavenly world (2:6), so the age to come has already begun to touch the present. Some scholars see in this a later, more settled view than in the undisputed letters; others point out that 2 Corinthians 5:17 and Galatians 1:4 already show the new age touching the present.
r: Romans 12:2; 1 Corinthians 2:6-8; Galatians 1:4; 2:6; Matthew 12:32; 4 Ezra 7:50; 2 Baruch 44:8-15

a: placed all things beneath his feet
t: Psalm 8:6: humanity's crown, now given to Christ
p: Psalm 8 praises humans as rulers; the New Testament sees it fulfilled in Jesus.
b: This is Psalm 8:6: "everything you have placed beneath his feet." In the psalm the "him" is humanity, crowned by God to rule creation. The New Testament reads it as true first of the man Jesus (1 Corinthians 15:27; Hebrews 2:6-9). Together with Psalm 110:1 in the verse before, it makes Christ both the king and the true human being who holds the rule given at creation. Ephesians keeps the "under his feet" for the powers (1:21) and then adds that he is given to the church as head.

a: head over all things
t: 'Head': ruler, source or both?
p: The Greek kephale can mean authority or source; the letter uses it more than once.
b: "Head" (kephale) is a body image here and in 4:15-16 and 5:23. Does it mean the one in authority (as most commentators and the context of 1:21-22 suggest) or the source from which the body grows (4:16)? Scholars have argued for both in the 5:23 debate. Here the first sense is plain: Christ is head "over all things" and "given to the church". The note at 5:23 (in the second part of this book) takes up the question of marriage.

a: the fullness of the one who is filling all things in every way
t: 'Fullness' (pleroma): who fills whom?
p: One of the hardest phrases in the letter: the church as the fullness of Christ.
b: The Greek pleroma means that which fills, or the filled state. The phrase has at least three readings. The church is filled by Christ. The church fills up, or completes, Christ, as a body completes a head (Calvin wrote that until Christ is united to us the Son of God "reckons himself in some measure imperfect"). Or Christ as the one filled with all of God's fullness (compare Colossians 1:19; 2:9) fills the church. The participle "filling" can also be a middle voice: Christ fills all things for himself. Paul returns to fullness in 3:19 and 4:13.

a: You were dead
t: Dead in trespasses: a picture of the old life
p: Paul calls the readers' former life death, though they were walking about.
b: Paul does not mean that the readers were physically dead. He is borrowing the biblical picture that sin cuts a person off from the source of life (Genesis 2:17; Isaiah 59:2; compare the father's words about the lost son in Luke 15:24). "Trespasses" (paraptomata, false steps) and "sins" (hamartiai, missing the mark) are two words for one condition. The same contrast of dead and alive runs through Romans 6:11-13 and Colossians 2:13. Churches differ on how far this "death" leaves the will free; the cards on 1:4 and 2:8 touch that question.

a: the ruler of the domain of the air
t: The ruler of the air: Satan and his realm
p: Paul's phrase for the devil appears nowhere else; it draws on ideas of the air as the lower heaven.
b: Most commentators take this ruler as Satan, called elsewhere "the god of this age" (2 Corinthians 4:4) and "ruler of this world" (John 12:31). "The domain of the air" fits an ancient picture in which the air between earth and the stars was filled with spirits; Philo wrote that the beings other philosophers call demons Moses usually calls angels, and that they are souls hovering in the air (On the Giants 6-9). Ignatius of Antioch, writing to Ephesus, speaks of "the prince of this world" (To the Ephesians 17:1; 19:1, in Lightfoot's translation). Clinton Arnold links the passage to Ephesus's magic and its belief in powers. Others read "the air" as the atmosphere of a godless culture. The Greek "authority" is singular and may mean the whole realm. The last phrase, "the spirit who is now active", is in the genitive in Greek, so it cannot simply stand beside "the ruler" (accusative); it most likely names the ruler's sphere or the spirit that works through him, and the Plain English Translation smooths this over.
orig: τὸν ἄρχοντα τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος (ton archonta tes exousias tou aeros)

a: children of anger
t: 'Children of anger by nature': what does it mean?
p: A Hebrew way of speaking, joined to the word 'by nature'; the churches read it differently.
b: "Children of" is a Hebrew idiom for belonging to a class ("children of disobedience", 2:2). "Anger" is God's settled opposition to sin (the Plain English Translation's term for orge). The disputed word is physei, "by nature". Augustine cited this verse for sin inherited from Adam, in his writings against the Pelagians (for example On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 2, which quotes Ephesians 2:3-5). Many modern commentators say Paul means only that all human beings, Jews included ("we all"), were in practice under God's anger, without a theory of how it began. The Romans note at 5:12 gives the churches' views on inherited sin.

a: gave us life together with Christ
t: Three 'with' verbs: made alive, raised, seated
p: Paul uses three words beginning 'together with': what Christ went through, believers go through.
b: In 2:5-6 three verbs begin with the prefix syn, "together with": syzoopoieo (give life together with), synegeiro (raise together with) and synkathizo (seat together with). They match what happened to Christ: life after death, resurrection, and a seat at God's right hand (1:20). Colossians 2:12-13 and 3:1 have the first two, but not the third. Romans 6 speaks of being buried and raised with Christ as something that happens in baptism, and puts the full resurrection in the future (Romans 6:5, 8). In Ephesians the raising is already done. See the note at 2:6.

a: seated us with him in the heavenly world
t: Already raised? A key point in the debate over authorship
p: Elsewhere Paul keeps believers' resurrection in the future; here it has happened.
b: In Romans 6:5 and 6:8 Paul says believers will be raised with Christ; here and in Colossians 2:12 they have been raised. Some scholars see here a shift that suggests a later writer, who has moved the hope from the future to the present. Defenders of Paul's authorship reply that Paul often holds a "now" and a "not yet" together (Romans 8:23-24; Philippians 3:12-14), and that Ephesians still looks ahead to "the day of redemption" (4:30) and "the ages to come" (2:7). Either way the Plain English Translation keeps the past tense: the three verbs are past, and the "heavenly world" is where Christ now is.
r: 1:20; 2:5; 4:30; Romans 6:5; Romans 6:8; Romans 8:23-24; Philippians 3:12-14; Colossians 2:12; Colossians 3:1

a: It is by grace that you have been saved, through faith.
t: Saved: already, and still
p: The verb is in the perfect tense: saved in the past, with the result lasting.
b: The Greek sesosmenoi este is a perfect participle with "you are": "you have been saved, and you are in the state of being saved." Elsewhere Paul can speak of salvation as past (Titus 3:5), present (1 Corinthians 1:18) or future (Romans 5:9-10; 13:11). Here Paul stresses the past and the lasting state. The two small phrases are the heart of the verse: "by grace" gives the cause, "through faith" the means. Faith is not the cause of the rescue; it is the open hand that receives it. The card below sets out how the churches have taught the relation of grace, faith and works.
orig: χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως (chariti este sesosmenoi dia pisteos)

a: This does not come from you.
t: 'This': faith, grace or the whole matter?
p: The Greek 'this' is neuter, while 'grace' and 'faith' are feminine; what does it point to?
b: "Grace" (charis) and "faith" (pistis) are both feminine in Greek, but "this" (touto) is neuter, so it does not agree with either. Three readings. (1) It refers to the whole matter of being saved by grace through faith; many commentators take this, since a neuter pronoun can point back to a whole thought. (2) It refers to faith, which would then be God's gift; Augustine quotes 2:8-10 in On the Spirit and the Letter while asking where faith itself comes from, and the Westminster Confession (14.1) calls the grace of faith the work of the Spirit of Christ in the hearts of the elect. (3) It refers to grace, though grace being a gift is already said. In every case Paul's point is the same: salvation does not come from human achievement.
r: Romans 3:24; Romans 4:4-5; Romans 6:23; Philippians 1:29; John 6:44; John 6:65

a: so that no one can boast
t: Works and boasting: what was Paul against?
p: Reformation readers heard 'earning salvation'; the New Perspective hears 'Jewish boundary-markers'.
b: For Luther and the Reformers, "works" meant any effort to earn God's favor, and Paul's target was the proud moral person. E. P. Sanders argued that first-century Judaism did not teach earning entry to the covenant: keeping the law was a way of staying in the covenant, not of getting in. Later scholars of the "New Perspective" argued that "boasting" in Paul's letters is mostly pride in the privileges that marked Jews off from Gentiles, such as circumcision and the food laws (Romans 3:27-30). Here the next section (2:11-22) is about exactly that division, which fits that reading. Catholic teaching, with Trent, reads grace as preceding and enabling all good works. The two readings do not exclude each other.

a: We are what he has made
t: Poiema: what God has made
p: The word is the root of the English 'poem': a thing made with care.
b: The Greek poiema means something made; the English words "poem" and "poetry" come from it. Paul uses it elsewhere only in Romans 1:20, of creation as God's work. The Greek Old Testament uses it for what God or humans have made (Ecclesiastes 3:11; Psalm 143:5, "your works"). The sense is that believers are God's handiwork, a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). It is not a claim that they are works of art, though many sermons say so. Verse 10 balances verse 9: no works to earn salvation, but good works as its purpose.

a: for us to walk in them
t: Walking: the Jewish picture of a way of life
p: 'Walk' means how one lives, as in the Hebrew word halakh and the later word halakhah.
b: The verb "walk" (peripateo) is a Hebrew idiom for how one lives. The Hebrew halak underlies the later Jewish word for the rules of life, halakhah, "the way to walk." Ephesians uses "walk" for the old life (2:2) and the new (2:10; 4:1, 17; 5:2, 8, 15). Here the letter says the good works were "prepared ahead of time", like a path laid out for them. Compare Psalm 1 and Deuteronomy 5:33, and Matthew 5:16.

a: The people called "the circumcision,
t: Jews and Gentiles: how each side named the other
p: Jews called Gentiles 'the uncircumcision', and Paul quotes the label with a gentle hint.
b: For Jews, circumcision was the sign of the covenant given to Abraham (Genesis 17:9-14), and "the uncircumcised" was a common word for non-Jews, often with scorn. Paul repeats the labels but with a pointed phrase: "made in the flesh by human hands". Elsewhere he says the real circumcision is of the heart and the Spirit (Romans 2:28-29; Philippians 3:3; Colossians 2:11). He writes as a Jew who knows the pride and the pain on both sides. Gentile believers need to hear that they were once outside, and Jewish believers that the sign alone does not keep them inside. Compare the Council of Jerusalem in Acts 15.
r: Genesis 17:9-14; Acts 15:1-29; Romans 2:28-29; Galatians 5:2-6; Philippians 3:3; Colossians 2:11

a: cut off from the commonwealth of Israel
t: Gentiles and the commonwealth of Israel
p: Gentiles were outside Israel's citizenship and covenants; now they are brought in.
b: The Greek politeia means citizenship, a constitution, or a people's way of life (Acts 22:28 uses it of Roman citizenship). "The covenants of the promise" are plural: with Abraham, at Sinai, with David (compare Romans 9:4). The five losses in the verse (no Christ, no citizenship, no covenants, no hope, no God) are the Gentiles' state before Christ. The text does not say Gentiles become a new Israel in place of Israel; it says they are admitted into Israel's commonwealth and share its promise (3:6). Whether that means a new people or a widened Israel is the question on which the churches differ. See the card at 3:6.

a: you were without God in the world
t: 'Without God': the word atheoi
p: The Greek 'atheoi' is the origin of 'atheists', but it does not mean what the English means.
b: This is the only use of atheoi in the New Testament. It describes the readers' former condition as lacking the true God, though they worshiped many gods (Acts 19:23-27 shows Ephesus's devotion to Artemis). Later the word turned back on the Christians: pagans called them "atheists" for refusing the city's gods, and a crowd in Smyrna shouted "Away with the atheists!" before the martyrdom of Polycarp (Martyrdom of Polycarp 3:2; 9:2). Paul's use is the opposite: the Gentiles were without the God of Israel; the Christians are not.

a: you who were once far away have come near
t: Isaiah 57:19: far and near
p: Paul reads the prophet's 'far and near' as Gentiles and Jews.
b: Isaiah 57:19 reads: "Peace, peace, to the one who is far and the one who is near." Paul quotes the passage in 2:17. In Isaiah, "far" and "near" probably meant Jews in exile and those at home. Later Jewish writers could use "near" for Gentiles who joined Israel, and some scholars think Paul has this use in mind. He turns it into a statement about the Gentiles who were far and are now brought near by the blood, and about the Jews who were near but still needed to be reconciled (2:16).

a: he broke down the middle wall
t: The middle wall: the Temple barrier and the law as a fence
p: Paul's picture of the wall probably recalls the barrier in the Jerusalem Temple.
b: The Greek mesotoichon tou phragmou means "the middle wall, the fence." Josephus tells of a stone barrier in the Jerusalem Temple with warning notices in Greek and Latin, forbidding any foreigner to go in on pain of death (Jewish War 5.193-194; 6.124-126). Two of the Greek notices have been found. When Paul was accused of taking Trophimus, an Ephesian, past the barrier, the crowd tried to kill him (Acts 21:27-36). A Jewish text of the third or early second century BC, the Letter of Aristeas (139-142), describes the law as a fence between Jews and the other peoples. Many scholars hold that both pictures lie behind the verse. The topic page on the dividing wall gives the evidence.
orig: τὸ μεσότοιχον τοῦ φραγμοῦ (to mesotoichon tou phragmou)

a: our peace
t: Christ is our peace: against the Roman peace
p: The empire advertised its peace; Paul says peace is a person.
b: Under Augustus the Roman state boasted that it had given the world peace, and the Altar of Augustan Peace (Ara Pacis) was dedicated in Rome in 9 BC. Cities in the province of Asia honored him as savior and bringer of good news. Paul's claim is that the real peace is not made by armies but by a crucified Jew, who brings two enemies into one body. The Hebrew prophets had named the coming king "Prince of Peace" (Isaiah 9:6) and said "this one will be peace" (Micah 5:5). Whether Paul intends a direct contrast with Rome is debated; some scholars think he does, while the nearer background is Isaiah.

a: put out of effect the law of commandments with its rules
t: Did Christ end the law of Moses?
p: The hardest sentence in the chapter: what exactly did he put out of effect?
b: The Greek katargeo means to make inoperative, to put out of effect, not to destroy. "The law of commandments in decrees" has been read in several ways. (1) The whole law of Moses as a system of rules. (2) Its ceremonial and boundary rules, circumcision, food and Sabbath, that fenced off Israel (the old division of moral, ceremonial and legal rules, and the New Perspective's "boundary markers"). (3) The Jewish traditions of interpretation built around the law as a fence. (4) The law as it condemned and divided, not the law as God's teaching. Compare Matthew 5:17-19 and Colossians 2:14. The card below places the churches side by side.
orig: τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασιν καταργήσας (ton nomon ton entolon en dogmasin katargesas)
r: Matthew 5:17-19; Romans 3:31; Romans 7:12; Galatians 3:23-25; Colossians 2:14; Colossians 2:20

a: one new humanity
t: One new humanity: the Adam and Christ picture
p: Paul's phrase is 'one new man'; the Plain English Translation says 'humanity' because the point is people, not a male.
b: The Greek kainos anthropos, "new person", takes up the Adam picture of Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15: Christ is the head of a new humanity. Paul uses the same phrase of the individual in 4:24 (where the Plain English Translation says "the new self") and in Colossians 3:10-11, and Galatians 3:28 speaks of "no Jew or Greek." In 2:15 the new person is a joint people in which neither Jew nor Gentile stays what they were. It is not Gentiles becoming Jews, nor Jews becoming Gentiles. Irenaeus's "recapitulation" (see 1:10) is one root of this reading. English versions that say "one new man" keep the Greek word anthropos, which here includes women.

a: to reconcile both to God in one body
t: Reconcile: a double verb found only in Ephesians and Colossians
p: Paul coins a stronger form of the usual verb: to reconcile completely.
b: The Greek apokatallasso adds a prefix to katallasso (to change from enmity to friendship, Romans 5:10; 2 Corinthians 5:18-20). Only Ephesians and Colossians use the longer form (Colossians 1:20, 22). The "one body" may mean Christ's crucified body, or the church; most commentators think both are meant. "Killed the hostility" is a violent image: the cross destroys the hatred itself, between Jew and Gentile and between each and God.

a: He came with the good news of peace
t: Isaiah 52:7 and 57:19 together
p: Paul joins the herald's good news of peace with 'far and near'.
b: Isaiah 52:7 praises the messenger "who brings good news, who makes peace heard", and Isaiah 57:19 speaks of peace for far and near. Paul joins them, and uses the verb euangelizomai, "to tell good news". When did Christ "come" and announce peace? Commentators take it of Jesus' earthly work (Acts 10:36 says God sent the message of peace through Jesus Christ), of his coming in the Spirit through the apostles' preaching, or of both. Roman ears knew the word too: an inscription from Priene in the province of Asia, about 9 BC, called the birthday of Augustus the beginning of "good news" for the world. The Plain English Translation uses "the good news" for the word, as everywhere.

a: both groups have access to the Father
t: Access: being brought into the presence
p: A court word for being introduced to a king; here all three persons of God are named.
b: The Greek prosagoge is the word for an introduction at court, the right to come in before a ruler. Romans 5:2 uses it of believers who stand in grace, and Ephesians 3:12 repeats it. Here all three persons of the later Christian creeds appear: through the Son, in the Spirit, to the Father. Many later writers on the Trinity have used the verse. In Jewish thought "drawing near" was what priests did in the temple, which gives this verse a priestly color: all believers, Jew and Gentile, may come near.

a: strangers and resident aliens
t: Strangers and aliens: the opposite of citizens
p: A resident alien lived in a city but without a citizen's rights.
b: A paroikos lived in a city without citizen rights and could be pushed out; he was a legal outsider. The Greek Old Testament uses the word for Israelites themselves in the land they did not own (Psalm 39:12) and for foreigners living among them. Gentile readers knew the difference between a citizen and a resident alien in their own cities, and would feel the point: God's city has no second-class residents. The Plain English Translation says "citizens together with the saints", a joint citizenship, and "God's household", which moves from law to family. Compare 1 Peter 2:11, where believers are called aliens in the world.

a: on the apostles and prophets as the foundation
t: 'Apostles and prophets': who, and why a foundation?
p: Does the verse mean Old Testament prophets or New Testament prophets? Are apostles still being laid?
b: Two groups, or one? The Greek puts both under a single article, which suggests a close pair. Most commentators take "prophets" as the New Testament prophets (3:5; 4:11; 1 Corinthians 12:28), so the foundation is the first generation of Christian witnesses; others add the Old Testament prophets. In 1 Corinthians 3:11 Paul says no one can lay another foundation than Christ, and Revelation 21:14 puts the twelve apostles' names on the city's foundations. The question for the churches is whether the foundation is complete and finished, so that apostles and prophets belong to the past, or whether the offices continue. Some who doubt Paul's authorship see here a later writer looking back to the apostolic age; defenders of Paul think he could say it himself. The card below gives the churches' views.

a: the cornerstone
t: Cornerstone or capstone?
p: The Greek akrogoniaios can mean the stone at the corner of the base or the stone at the top.
b: The Greek akrogoniaios is a word found in Isaiah 28:16 in the Greek Old Testament, where the Plain English Translation reads "a cornerstone of great worth" (Isaiah 28:16). In building, a cornerstone was laid first and set the lines of the walls. Joachim Jeremias argued that here it means the capstone at the top, which completes the building; most commentators keep "cornerstone", since the next verses speak of growth from the foundation. Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22 of himself (Matthew 21:42), and 1 Peter 2:6-8 uses both Isaiah and the psalm. The image of Christ as foundation, stone and head of the corner recurs throughout the New Testament.

a: the whole building
t: 'The whole building' or 'every building'?
p: The Greek has no article, so it could say 'every building'; the KJV ("all the building") adds one.
b: The Greek is pasa oikodome without the article, which literally means "every building" or "every structure". The KJV reads "all the building", as if the Greek had the article. Most commentators take the sense as "the whole building", one structure; a few hold that Paul pictures many local churches, each a building, all growing into one temple. The verb "grows" is odd for a building, and it mixes the picture of a house with the picture of a body (4:16).

a: a temple
t: The church as God's temple
p: The word naos names the sanctuary where God dwells; the community now takes its place.
b: The Greek naos is the inner sanctuary, the place where God lived, and not the whole temple area (hieron). The idea that a community is God's temple is old. The Qumran community described itself as a holy house for Israel and a foundation of the holy of holies for Aaron, in place of what it saw as a defiled Temple (Community Rule 8). Paul uses it for the church (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; 2 Corinthians 6:16) and for the body of the individual believer (1 Corinthians 6:19). For readers in Ephesus the point had extra bite, with its great temple of Artemis, and with the Jerusalem temple that Gentiles could not enter beyond the court (see 2:14).

a: a home for God in the Spirit
t: God's dwelling: from tent to people
p: God had said he would live among his people; here the people themselves are his home.
b: In Exodus 25:8 the LORD says, "They are to make me a holy place, and I will live in their midst", and Psalm 132:13 sings of Zion as the place he "has longed to make it his home". The word katoiketerion is the dwelling place. The line completes the movement of the chapter: from tent to temple, from temple to people, from one nation to Jews and Gentiles together. The three persons are again named: the Lord (Christ) in 2:21, the Spirit, and God.

a: the prisoner of Christ Jesus
t: Paul in prison: where?
p: The letter says Paul is a prisoner, but not where; the choices are Rome, Caesarea or Ephesus.
b: Paul calls himself a prisoner here and in 4:1 and 6:20 ("an ambassador in chains"). Acts tells of two long periods of custody: about two years at Caesarea (Acts 23:33-26:32) and two years under guard in Rome (Acts 28:16-31). Many scholars date Ephesians to Rome; some prefer Caesarea. A third view puts the letters from prison (Philippians, Colossians, Philemon, perhaps Ephesians) in Ephesus, since Paul spoke of many imprisonments (2 Corinthians 11:23), and 1 Clement 5:6 says he was in chains seven times, though Acts does not tell of an Ephesian imprisonment. If a follower of Paul wrote the letter after his death, "prisoner" is part of the portrait of the apostle.
r: 4:1; 6:20; Acts 23:33-26:32; Acts 28:16-31; 2 Corinthians 11:23; Philippians 1:12-14; Colossians 4:3; Philemon 1:9

a: you Gentiles
t: A sentence that breaks off
p: Paul begins a prayer, stops in the middle, and does not return to it until verse 14.
b: The sentence that begins "For this reason I, Paul..." never finishes; Paul interrupts himself with a long digression (3:2-13) and starts again at 3:14 with the same words "for this reason". Greek teachers called this anacoluthon, a broken construction. Many readers find it natural in dictated speech; it also shows how the letter's thought flows from one idea into the next. Verse 1 refers back to chapter 2, to the union of Jews and Gentiles that Paul's own imprisonment serves.

a: If you have indeed heard
t: 'If indeed you have heard': what does Paul assume?
p: The Greek 'if indeed' can express certainty or doubt.
b: The Greek eige ("if indeed") can mean "since" (taking it for granted), or "if, as I assume" (leaving a doubt). It would be strange for Paul to doubt that Ephesians had heard of his work, since he lived among them for three years (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31). This is one of the passages that make scholars ask who the first readers were: Christians in Asia he had never met (Colossians 2:1 speaks so of Laodicea), a circular letter, or readers of a later generation who knew him only by report. See the note at 1:15.

a: the task of managing God's grace
t: Stewardship: the household manager
p: The same word as 'plan' in 1:10, here Paul's own job.
b: The Greek oikonomia was the job of a household manager, often a trusted slave who ran an estate for the owner. Paul sees himself as God's manager, given the job of distributing God's grace to the Gentiles. Compare 1 Corinthians 4:1-2 ("managers of God's secrets") and Colossians 1:25. The same Greek word is the "plan" of 1:10 and 3:9: Paul manages what God planned. See the note at 1:10.

a: as I wrote briefly before
t: 'As I wrote briefly before': which writing?
p: Paul points back to an earlier statement; it is not clear where.
b: Three possibilities. He may mean earlier in this letter, 1:9-10 and 2:11-22, where he has already spoken of the mystery. He may mean an earlier letter now lost, or a letter such as Colossians (Colossians 1:26-27; 2:2). Or, if a later writer is speaking, he may mean Paul's earlier letters generally (Romans 16:25-26; 1 Corinthians 2:7-10). The first is the most natural: "briefly" fits a short earlier statement in the same letter, and "when you read it" in 3:4 invites the reader to go back.

a: it was not made known to human beings
t: Was the mystery hidden in the Old Testament?
p: The prophets did foretell the nations coming in; what is new here?
b: The Old Testament already promised that the nations would be blessed through Abraham (Genesis 12:3), that the servant would be "a light to the nations" (Isaiah 49:6), and that the temple would be "a house of prayer for all the peoples" (Isaiah 56:7). Romans 16:26 even says the mystery is made known "through the writings of the prophets." So Paul's "not made known" here is read as a comparison, "not made known as it has now been": the truth was hinted, but its full shape, Gentiles fully equal with Jews without becoming Jews, was not known until now. The Greek has hos, "as", and the Plain English Translation keeps the comparison: "in the way it has now been unveiled". Whether the church was seen at all in the Old Testament is a point on which covenant and dispensational readers differ.

a: The mystery is that the Gentiles
t: The secret: Gentiles as equal heirs
p: What exactly is the mystery? That Gentiles are saved, or that they are joined to Israel on equal terms?
b: That the nations would come to the God of Israel was no secret. What Paul calls new is that Gentiles share fully, as Gentiles, in Israel's inheritance with no need to become Jews first. The churches draw different conclusions about what this means for Israel. Covenant theology (Calvin and the Reformed): one people of God, now widened; the church as Israel's heir. Catholic teaching (Lumen Gentium 9; Nostra Aetate 4): the church draws life from Israel's root, and God does not take back the gifts and the call he gave the Jews. Dispensationalist teaching: Israel and the church have distinct roles, and the church belongs to a separate program, a "mystery". The card below sets these out.

a: heirs together, members of the body together, and sharers together
t: Three 'together' words
p: Three Greek words start with 'syn': the readers share everything with Israel.
b: The Greek has three compounds beginning with syn ("together with"): synkleronoma (fellow heirs; compare Romans 8:17), sussoma (fellow members of the body) and symmetocha (fellow sharers). Of these, sussoma is not found elsewhere in the New Testament. The word symmetocha returns in 5:7. The stress on being "together with" Israel matches 2:19, "citizens together with the saints". English cannot give each its own word, so the Plain English Translation repeats "together" at the end of each.
orig: συγκληρονόμα καὶ σύσσωμα καὶ συμμέτοχα (synkleronoma kai sussoma kai symmetocha)

a: less than the least of all the saints
t: 'Less than the least': Paul's self-description
p: A double comparison: Paul puts himself below the lowest.
b: Paul coins a comparative on a superlative: elachistoteros, "more least". In 1 Corinthians 15:9 he is "the least of the apostles", and in 1 Timothy 1:15 the foremost of sinners. Because he persecuted the church, his humility is more than a manner of speaking. Some scholars hear here a later writer building up Paul's image as the great apostle to the Gentiles; others hear Paul's own startled wonder at being chosen. The word "saints" (see the note at 1:1) includes all believers, so he is not placing himself below a special class.

a: kept hidden from the ages in God
t: Hidden in God from the ages
p: God's plan was not unknown to God: it was held back until now.
b: The mystery was "kept hidden" (a perfect participle: hidden and still hidden until revealed) "in God". Compare Romans 16:25 ("kept in silence for long ages"), 1 Corinthians 2:7 and Colossians 1:26. The phrase "who created all things" ties the plan to creation: the one who made the world also planned its gathering in Christ (1:10). The Byzantine text and the KJV add "through Jesus Christ" at the end of the verse (see the variant).

a: the rulers and authorities in the heavenly world
t: The church shows the powers God's wisdom
p: How can a church teach angels or demons anything?
b: The same words as in 1:21 and 6:12: "rulers and authorities". Here they are being taught "through the church", by the sight of Jews and Gentiles made one. Are they good angels who rejoice at it (compare 1 Peter 1:12) or hostile powers who see their rule ending (Colossians 2:15)? Many modern commentators take them as hostile or at least as unfriendly powers that had kept the nations divided; Calvin took them as the heavenly angels, who had not known the gospel's mercy to the Gentiles until now; Chrysostom (Homily 7 on Ephesians) has Paul claim to enlighten angels and archangels, and says the phrase covers both the powers above and those beneath. Clinton Arnold reads them against the many powers Ephesians feared in their magic and astrology. Others add human structures. The church's role is to be a living sign of what the powers cannot do: unite what they divided.
orig: ταῖς ἀρχαῖς καὶ ταῖς ἐξουσίαις (tais archais kai tais exousiais)

a: richly varied wisdom
t: Wisdom of many colors
p: A rare Greek word for something woven in many colors.
b: The Greek polypoikilos appears only here in the New Testament. It comes from poikilos, "many-colored", used of embroidered cloth and of the many hues of a flower bed; the Greek Old Testament uses a related word for Joseph's coat of many colors (Genesis 37:3). God's wisdom is neither plain nor single: it is a design woven of many threads, in this case the joining of two peoples. Compare Romans 11:33, "Oh, how deep are God's riches, his wisdom and his knowledge!" (Romans 11:33).

a: freedom of speech and access
t: Confident entry into God's presence
p: Two terms from the world of the royal court: free speech and being introduced.
b: "Freedom of speech" (parresia) was a citizen's right to speak openly in the assembly, and "access" (prosagoge) is the introduction to a ruler (see 2:18). Together with "confidence" they describe how believers may come to God. On "faith in him" (dia tes pisteos autou): the Greek can also be read "through his faithfulness", the faithfulness of Christ. As at Romans 3:22 the Plain English Translation follows the reading "faith in him". Scholars divide: some argue for "his faithfulness", others for "faith in him". The same question arises at Galatians 2:16 and Philippians 3:9.
orig: διὰ τῆς πίστεως αὐτοῦ (dia tes pisteos autou)

a: So I ask that you not lose heart
t: Who asks, and who might lose heart?
p: The infinitive "to lose heart" has no stated subject: Paul may be asking God not to let him lose heart.
b: The infinitive "to lose heart" has no stated subject. Either Paul asks his readers not to lose heart over his imprisonment (the Plain English Translation's reading, which most translations take), or he asks God that he himself not lose heart, which would lead into the prayer of 3:14. His troubles are "your glory", because the Gentile mission that landed him in prison is what has made them part of God's people. Compare Colossians 1:24 and 2 Corinthians 4:17.

a: I kneel
t: Kneeling in prayer
p: Jews usually prayed standing; kneeling marks an urgent or humble prayer.
b: The usual Jewish posture for prayer was standing, with hands raised (1 Kings 8:22; Mark 11:25). Kneeling marks intense or humble prayer: Solomon at the temple dedication (1 Kings 8:54), Daniel (Daniel 6:10), Jesus in Gethsemane (Luke 22:41), Stephen (Acts 7:60), and Paul at Miletus and Tyre (Acts 20:36; 21:5). Here Paul turns from his digression to a second great prayer. The Byzantine text and the KJV add "of our Lord Jesus Christ" after "Father" (see the variant).
r: 1 Kings 8:22; 1 Kings 8:54; Daniel 6:10; Luke 22:41; Acts 7:60; Acts 20:36; Acts 21:5; Philippians 2:10

a: every family in heaven and on earth gets its name
t: A play on words: patria and pater
p: The Greek 'family' (patria) comes from 'father' (pater): all fatherhood comes from God.
b: Greek has pater (father) and patria (a family or clan traced to a father). Paul's wordplay says that every family takes its name and its being from the Father; English can only show it by explaining. The KJV reads "the whole family in heaven and earth", but without the article the Greek means "every family". The Greek Old Testament of Genesis 12:3 says "tribes of the earth" (phylai), but Acts 3:25, quoting the promise to Abraham, has patriai, "families", so the sentence may hint at that promise. Augustus was titled "father of the fatherland" (pater patriae) in 2 BC: Paul may be answering such claims.

a: your inner self
t: The inner self
p: A phrase Paul uses for the self that is renewed, even as the outer wears away.
b: The same Greek phrase is in Romans 7:22, where Paul delights in the law of God in his "inner self"; 2 Corinthians 4:16 is a close parallel, where "our inner self" is renewed day by day while the outer wears away. Plato had already spoken of "the man within" for the reasoning self (Republic 589a, in Jowett's translation). Paul does not teach a Greek division of soul from body here; he means the person as God sees and renews him. The Spirit works there, and Christ makes his home in the heart (3:17).

a: Christ would settle in your hearts
t: Christ settles in: katoikeo
p: A word for settling permanently, the opposite of staying as a guest.
b: The Greek katoikeo means to settle down and live in a place, to be at home. It is the opposite of paroikos in 2:19: Gentiles who were "resident aliens" in God's city now have Christ living in their hearts. Colossians 1:19 uses it of God's fullness living in Christ. "Rooted" is a plant image and "founded" a building image, joined as in 2:20-21 and Colossians 2:7.

a: what the width and length and height and depth are
t: The four dimensions: of what?
p: Paul gives four measures but does not say what is measured.
b: The Greek has no object: "what is the width and length and height and depth". Readings include Christ's love (3:19), God's wisdom or the mystery (3:9-10), the cosmos, the church as the temple of 2:21, or the cross. Augustine, in his Letter 55, quoted this verse and saw the shape of the cross in the four dimensions. Job 11:7-9 uses similar measures for the depth of God, which no one can find out. The idea that the saints grasp it "together" is important: Paul pictures a community, not a lone mystic, who comes to know it.

a: though it goes beyond knowing
t: To know what is beyond knowing
p: A paradox: Paul prays that they know a love that exceeds knowledge.
b: Paul prays for the readers to know a love that is bigger than anything a person can know. The same figure appears at Philippians 4:7 (the peace that goes beyond understanding). Biblical "knowing" is not just information but closeness. The paradox is not an escape from thought: it means that love can be known truly without being known completely, as a child knows a parent.

a: filled up to all the fullness of God
t: 'Filled with all the fullness of God': how far?
p: Does Paul speak of growth, of maturity, or of sharing in God's own life?
b: It is a stunning prayer, and readers have measured it differently. Some readers hear in "filled with all the fullness of God" the language of sharing in God's own life, and can compare 2 Peter 1:4. Catholic teaching speaks of divinization in general: the Catechism (460) quotes the line "the Son of God became man so that we might become God" (its note names Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54, and Aquinas, Opusculum 57). Readers may also take the verse as a prayer for spiritual maturity and the abundance of what God supplies. The "fullness" ties to 1:23 (the church as Christ's fullness) and 4:13 (the "measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ").

a: to him belongs the glory
t: A doxology to close the first half
p: Paul ends with praise, as Romans 11:36 does.
b: A doxology (a short praise to God) closes each half of the letter's first major section and is a pattern in Paul: Romans 11:36; 16:27; Galatians 1:5; Philippians 4:20. It ends with "Amen", the Hebrew word for "so be it". The oddity is the order "in the church and in Christ Jesus": the church is named first. The glory of God is given in the church and in Christ; the church's own life is where the praise is voiced. The Byzantine text omits one "and" (see the variant). Chapters 1 to 3 are the doctrinal half of the letter; chapters 4 to 6 turn to conduct.
